propositions.text: Transfer pricing issues arise when multinational entities transfer property or services without arm's length dealings, risking profit diversion.
Since 1939, Income Tax Act allows reassessment to include differences between non-arm's length prices and arm's length prices.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains transfer pricing issues and the Income Tax Act's reassessment provisions since 1939.

propositions.text: Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada for 1990-1993 under s. 69(2) for paying above arm's length price for ranitidine.
Reassessment increased Glaxo Canada's income by difference between highest generic company price and Glaxo's price.
Glaxo Canada appealed to Tax Court, which upheld reassessment with minor revision.
Federal Court of Appeal allowed Glaxo Canada's appeal and remitted to Tax Court for reconsideration.
Minister appealed Federal Court of Appeal decision to this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada; Tax Court upheld; Federal Court of Appeal allowed appeal; Minister now appeals to this Court.

propositions.text: Issue is correct application of s. 69(2), especially circumstances to consider for reasonable arm's length price.
Glaxo Canada cross-appeals Federal Court of Appeal's remittal, arguing no remittal needed as Minister's assumptions demolished.
Court would dismiss both Minister's appeal and Glaxo Canada's cross-appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue and that it would dismiss both the Minister's appeal and Glaxo Canada's cross-appeal.

propositions.text: Between 1990-1993, Glaxo Canada bought ranitidine from related non-resident Adechsa at $1,512-$1,651/kg.
Two Canadian generic companies bought ranitidine from other sources at $194-$304/kg during same period.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada bought ranitidine from related Adechsa at high prices; generic companies bought at much lower prices.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada was wholly owned by Glaxo Group Ltd., itself owned by Glaxo Holdings plc UK.
Glaxo Group owned other companies discovering, developing, manufacturing, marketing branded pharmaceuticals.
Products marketed worldwide through subsidiaries like Glaxo Canada or independent distributors.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada was a wholly owned subsidiary of Glaxo Group Ltd., which was owned by Glaxo Holdings plc UK, marketing pharmaceuticals worldwide.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada was secondary manufacturer and marketer, acquiring ranitidine and marketing Zantac under patent and trademark rights.
Glaxo Group owned Zantac trademark and patent, granting rights to Glaxo Canada under Licence Agreement.
Glaxo Canada purchased ranitidine from Adechsa under Supply Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada manufactured and marketed Zantac under licence from Glaxo Group and purchased ranitidine from Adechsa under Supply Agreement.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement granted Glaxo Canada multiple rights including patents, trademarks, technical assistance, marketing support, indemnification, sublicensing.

paragraphs.summary: Licence Agreement conferred numerous rights and benefits on Glaxo Canada including patents, trademarks, technical help, marketing support, and indemnification.

propositions.text: Supply Agreement set transfer prices using resale-price method with 60% gross margin for distributors.
Example: if product sold for $10, transfer price $4; if $20, transfer price $8.
Appellant's counsel described pricing as starting from in-market price minus gross profit margin to determine transfer price and royalties.
This method resulted in prices over $1,500/kg for ranitidine paid by Glaxo Canada to Adechsa.
Combined Licence and Supply agreements enabled Glaxo Canada to purchase ranitidine, package, and market Zantac.

paragraphs.summary: Supply Agreement used resale-price method setting transfer prices; combined agreements enabled Glaxo Canada to market Zantac.

propositions.text: Apotex and Novopharm sold generic anti-ulcer drugs, buying ranitidine at $194-$304/kg from arm's length suppliers.
No evidence their supply contracts conferred benefits beyond supply of ranitidine.

paragraphs.summary: Generic companies bought ranitidine at lower prices from arm's length suppliers without additional contractual benefits.

propositions.text: Generic companies marketed generic drugs under compulsory licensing scheme existing until Feb 1993, paying royalties to patent owner.
Licences granted before Dec 20, 1991, continued despite repeal of compulsory licensing in 1993.

paragraphs.summary: Generic companies marketed drugs under compulsory licensing paying royalties; licences before Dec 1991 continued after repeal.

propositions.text: Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada increasing income by $51 million under s. 69(2) for paying more than reasonable for ranitidine.

paragraphs.summary: Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada increasing income by $51 million for overpaying for ranitidine.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. affirmed Minister’s reassessment.
Singleton v. Canada requires Licence and Supply agreements to be considered independently.
Did not consider Licence Agreement rights relevant to arm’s length price for ranitidine supply.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. affirmed reassessment, applying Singleton to consider Licence and Supply agreements independently, excluding Licence Agreement rights.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. used comparable uncontrolled price (CUP) method per OECD Guidelines to test reasonableness of transactions.
Appropriate comparator was highest price paid by generic companies to arm’s length suppliers.
Prices Glaxo Canada paid to Adechsa were greater than reasonable arm’s length amount.
Allowed $25/kg increment for granulation but upheld reassessment.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. applied CUP method, found Glaxo Canada paid more than reasonable price, allowed minor increment, upheld reassessment.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal found Tax Court erred by not considering Licence Agreement in price reasonableness under s. 69(2).
Singleton not relevant; test includes all circumstances an arm’s length purchaser would consider.
Adopted 'reasonable business person' test from Gabco Ltd. requiring inquiry into relevant circumstances for price decision.
Rip A.C.J. erred assessing fair market value based on generic companies’ prices.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal held Tax Court erred excluding Licence Agreement, adopted reasonable business person test, rejected generic prices as comparator.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement central to Glaxo Canada’s business reality and must be considered in price reasonableness.
Tax Court erred using generic companies’ prices as Licence Agreement created fundamentally different circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal found Licence Agreement central and Tax Court erred using generic prices due to different circumstances.

propositions.text: Taxpayer burden not fully discharged; reasonable amount for Glaxo Canada’s ranitidine transactions remains to be determined.
Matter remitted to Tax Court for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal found taxpayer burden not discharged and remitted matter to Tax Court for redetermination.

propositions.text: First transfer pricing provision enacted in 1939 as s. 23B of Income War Tax Act, re-enacted in 1948 and 1952 Acts.
Section 17(3) of 1952 Act similar to s. 69(2) enacted in 1971 with minor 1985 modifications.

paragraphs.summary: Court outlines history of transfer pricing provisions from 1939 to 1985 versions of Income Tax Act.

propositions.text: 1985 s. 69(2) provides reassessment if taxpayer pays more than reasonable amount to non-arm’s length non-resident.
Reasonable amount is what would be reasonable if parties dealt at arm’s length in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Court states 1985 s. 69(2) allows reassessment if payment exceeds reasonable arm’s length amount in circumstances.

propositions.text: Question is whether Glaxo Canada paid more than reasonable arm’s length price for ranitidine from Adechsa.
Challenge is to find arm’s length proxy replicating Glaxo Canada’s acquisition circumstances closely.

paragraphs.summary: Court frames issue as whether Glaxo Canada paid more than reasonable arm’s length price and finding suitable proxy.

propositions.text: 1979 and 1995 OECD Guidelines referenced but not controlling like Canadian statute.
Test of transactions must be determined by s. 69(2), not by Guidelines’ methodology or commentary.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes OECD Guidelines are referenced but s. 69(2) governs test, not Guidelines’ methods.

propositions.text: Section 69(2) does not specify how to determine the reasonable amount payable at arm's length.
The Guidelines suggest methods to check if transfer prices align with arm's length prices.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 69(2) lacks guidance on reasonable amount determination; Guidelines suggest methods for arm's length price consistency.

propositions.text: In Tax Court, parties used four Guidelines methods to assess Glaxo Canada's prices to Adechsa.
Minister relied on CUP and cost plus methods per 1979 Guidelines.
CUP compares prices in comparable arm's length transactions with taxpayer's transfer prices.
Minister compared Glaxo Canada's prices with Apotex and Novopharm using CUP method.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains parties used four methods; Minister used CUP and cost plus; CUP compares comparable arm's length prices; Minister compared Glaxo prices with generic companies.

propositions.text: 1995 Guidelines require arm's length transactions to be comparable for price comparison.
Transactions are comparable if differences don't materially affect price or adjustments can eliminate effects.

paragraphs.summary: The court states 1995 Guidelines require comparability of arm's length transactions, with no material price effects or adjustable differences.

propositions.text: Cost plus method uses supplier costs plus mark-up but has issues assessing costs and mark-up.
1979 Guidelines suggest cost plus is useful to verify prices after other methods.
Minister used cost plus to verify arm's length prices determined by CUP method.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes cost plus method's issues; 1979 Guidelines say it's useful for verification; Minister used it to verify CUP prices.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada used resale price, transactional net margin, and CUP methods with European comparators.
Resale price method starts with reseller's market price minus reseller's cost and profit margin to find transfer price.
1979 Guidelines say resale price method is useful for marketing operations.
Glaxo Canada compared its gross profit margin with independent European distributors of Zantac.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada used resale price, transactional net margin, and CUP methods; resale price method explained; 1979 Guidelines find it useful; Glaxo compared margins with European distributors.

propositions.text: Transactional net margin method compares net profit ratios in controlled and uncontrolled transactions or independent enterprises.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains transactional net margin method compares net profit ratios in controlled and uncontrolled or independent transactions.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada's CUP approach used prices paid by European independent distributors approximating prices paid to Adechsa.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada submitted its CUP approach used European independent distributor prices approximating those paid to Adechsa.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. rejected Glaxo Canada's evidence and submissions.
Using CUP, Rip A.C.J. found generic companies paid about $300/kg, Glaxo Canada paid over $1,500/kg.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. rejected Glaxo Canada's evidence and found Glaxo paid over $1,500/kg versus generics' $300/kg using CUP method.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada argued comparison with generic companies was inappropriate due to Licence Agreement rights and benefits.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada argued generic company comparison was inappropriate because Licence Agreement conferred rights and benefits.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. found Singleton precluded considering Licence Agreement.
Without Licence Agreement, prices under Supply Agreement were only for ranitidine, no compensation for other rights.
No differences justified higher transfer prices than Apotex and Novopharm prices, except $25/kg granulation charge allowed.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. found Singleton barred Licence Agreement consideration; prices were only for ranitidine; no justification for higher prices except $25/kg granulation.

propositions.text: Question was whether Licence Agreement was a circumstance to consider in determining reasonable price under s. 69(2).

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. faced the issue whether Licence Agreement should be considered in determining reasonable price under s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Minister argues Singleton, Shell, and Guidelines require transactional approach for s. 69(2) reasonable transfer price.
Minister says transaction-by-transaction approach treats each transaction independently, making Licence Agreement irrelevant.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues Singleton, Shell, and Guidelines require transactional approach treating each transaction independently, excluding Licence Agreement.

propositions.text: Minister submits Singleton and Shell under s. 20(1)(c)(i) require transaction-by-transaction approach under s. 69(2).
Singleton involved deductibility of interest under s. 20(1)(c)(i) where borrowed funds' use was key issue.
Singleton found borrowed funds used to invest in law firm for income earning; borrowing to buy house irrelevant.
Rip A.C.J. said s. 69(2) requires Supply and Licence agreements to be treated separately due to transaction separation.

paragraphs.summary: Minister submits Singleton and Shell require transaction-by-transaction approach; Singleton involved interest deductibility; Rip A.C.J. treated Supply and Licence agreements separately.

propositions.text: Tax Court judge and Minister ignore difference between s. 20(1)(c)(i) and s. 69(2).
s. 20(1)(c)(i) only requires factual determination of borrowed funds' use for income earning.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Tax Court judge and Minister ignore difference between s. 20(1)(c)(i) and s. 69(2); s. 20(1)(c)(i) requires only factual use determination.

propositions.text: s. 20(1)(c)(i) does not require reasonableness or transaction comparison for interest deduction.
s. 69(2) requires determining if transfer price was greater than reasonable amount had parties dealt at arm's length.
If other transactions are relevant to s. 69(2), they must not be ignored.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 20(1)(c)(i) lacks reasonableness test; s. 69(2) requires assessing if price exceeds reasonable arm's length amount; relevant transactions must be considered.

propositions.text: Shell involved s. 20(1)(c)(i) and whether borrowed funds were used to earn income.
Shell borrowed NZ$150 million at 15.4%, converted to US$, used for business; currency transactions reduced effective interest to 9.1%.

paragraphs.summary: Shell involved s. 20(1)(c)(i) and use of borrowed funds; Shell borrowed NZ$150M at 15.4%, converted to US$, reducing effective interest to 9.1%.

propositions.text: Shell issue was whether converted funds were used to earn income despite tax scheme.
Court found conversion irrelevant; Minister cannot re-characterize bona fide legal relationships.

paragraphs.summary: Shell issue was use of converted funds; court found conversion irrelevant and Minister cannot re-characterize bona fide relationships.

propositions.text: s. 69(2) requires redetermining price as if parties dealt at arm's length, considering other transactions if relevant.
Shell is inapplicable to s. 69(2) determinations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 69(2) requires price redetermination considering other transactions; Shell is inapplicable to s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Minister relied on 1995 Guidelines para. 1.42 to justify transaction-by-transaction approach.
Minister submits para. 1.42 requires focusing only on particular transaction, excluding Licence Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: Minister relies on 1995 Guidelines para. 1.42 to justify transaction-by-transaction approach excluding Licence Agreement.

propositions.text: Para. 1.42 is not as restrictive; recognizes some transactions are linked and cannot be evaluated separately.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds para. 1.42 recognizes linked transactions may not be evaluated separately, limiting transaction-by-transaction approach.

propositions.text: 1995 Guidelines state arm’s length principle compares controlled transactions with independent enterprises’ transactions.
Economically relevant characteristics must be sufficiently comparable for useful comparison.
Differences must not materially affect the condition examined or must be adjusted for.

paragraphs.summary: The 1995 Guidelines explain the arm’s length principle requires sufficiently comparable economically relevant characteristics for controlled and independent transactions, per prior authority.

propositions.text: Proper arm’s length application requires regard to economically relevant characteristics to ensure comparability.
Transaction-by-transaction approach may be appropriate if no related transactions or irrelevant related transactions.
Relevant circumstances must be considered to decide if other transactions impacting transfer price should be included.

paragraphs.summary: The court states arm’s length principle requires considering economically relevant characteristics and relevant circumstances to decide if related transactions affect transfer price.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. erred in finding he was precluded from considering the Licence Agreement.
Whether Rip A.C.J. should have considered the Licence Agreement remains a question.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Rip A.C.J. erred in excluding the Licence Agreement but questions if he should have considered it.

propositions.text: Section 69(2) requires inquiry into reasonable price had parties dealt at arm’s length, considering all relevant circumstances.
Circumstances include linked agreements conferring rights and benefits beyond property purchase.
Objective is to determine arm’s length price for property plus linked rights and benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 69(2) requires considering all relevant circumstances, including linked agreements, to find arm’s length price for property and benefits.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada’s business was secondary manufacturing and marketing of brand-name pharmaceuticals including Zantac.
Glaxo Canada engaged in R&D but not related to Zantac.
Glaxo Canada’s purchase of ranitidine must be understood in this business context.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Glaxo Canada’s business involved secondary manufacturing and marketing, with unrelated R&D, framing its ranitidine purchase context.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. found appellant required by Licence Agreement to purchase ranitidine from Glaxo approved sources.
Parties do not dispute Rip A.C.J.’s finding on purchase requirement.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. found and parties agree appellant had to buy ranitidine from Glaxo approved sources per Licence Agreement.

propositions.text: Only two approved sources existed, one being Adechsa.
To benefit from Licence Agreement, Glaxo Canada had to buy active ingredient from these sources.
Requirement arose from Glaxo Group’s control of trademark and patent, not from non-arm’s length relationship.
An arm’s length distributor might face the same requirement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Glaxo Canada had to buy from approved sources due to Glaxo Group’s trademark and patent control, a requirement arm’s length distributors might face.

propositions.text: Link between Licence and Supply agreements meant marketers of Zantac faced contractual price terms not faced by generic ranitidine marketers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Licence and Supply agreements linked contractual price terms to Zantac marketers unlike generic ranitidine marketers.

propositions.text: Rights and benefits of Licence Agreement were contingent on Glaxo Canada entering Supply Agreement with Glaxo Group designated suppliers.
Price paid allocated compensation to Glaxo Canada for secondary manufacturing and marketing function.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Licence Agreement rights depended on Supply Agreement with designated suppliers, allocating compensation for Glaxo Canada’s function.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. was concerned multinationals could avoid arm’s length price measurement by requiring Canadian subsidiaries to buy from specified suppliers.
Whatever price Glaxo Group set is subject to s. 69(2) requiring arm’s length measurement.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. worried about avoidance of arm’s length pricing, but court finds s. 69(2) still applies to prices set by Glaxo Group.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada paid for some Licence Agreement rights as part of ranitidine purchase price from Adechsa.
Licence Agreement cannot be ignored in determining reasonable amount paid under s. 69(2), which covers goods and services.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Licence Agreement rights were paid for in ranitidine price and must be considered under s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Considering Licence and Supply agreements together gives realistic picture of Glaxo Canada’s profits.
Glaxo Canada’s function was secondary manufacturing and marketing, not product origination or associated risks.
Prices paid to Adechsa included payment for some Licence Agreement rights and product under Supply Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds combined Licence and Supply agreements reflect Glaxo Canada’s secondary role and payments for rights and product.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. erred in refusing to consider Licence Agreement.
Refusal led to finding generic companies’ prices comparable under CUP method.
Generic comparators do not reflect Glaxo Canada’s economic reality and do not indicate reasonable price without adjustment.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees Rip A.C.J. erred excluding Licence Agreement, causing flawed CUP comparison ignoring Glaxo Canada’s economic reality.

propositions.text: Reasonable amount if Glaxo Canada and Adechsa dealt at arm’s length remains undetermined.
Determination requires close examination of Licence Agreement terms and rights granted.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees reasonable arm’s length price is undetermined and requires close Licence Agreement examination.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement clause 11(1)(b) states no royalties payable by Glaxo Canada on purchase of raw materials or products from Group or Associates.
Royalties payable only on Glaxo Canada’s net sales, not on importation or manufacture.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Licence Agreement clauses specify no royalties on purchases, only on net sales by Glaxo Canada.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada did not rely on tax provisions for royalties or withholding tax in pleadings.
No evidence Glaxo Canada withheld amounts for royalties to Adechsa.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Glaxo Canada did not rely on tax provisions and no evidence of withholding royalties to Adechsa.

propositions.text: No determination made whether patent and trademark rights are linked to purchase price paid to Adechsa.
If purchase price includes intellectual property compensation, consistency with withholding tax position is required.
Issue not argued here; may be addressed in Tax Court later.

paragraphs.summary: The court makes no determination on IP rights linkage to price, notes consistency with withholding tax needed, and defers issue to Tax Court.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement grants other rights and benefits beyond patent and trademark, e.g. access to new products, supply, marketing support, technical assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Licence Agreement grants various rights and benefits beyond patent and trademark rights.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. found ranitidine and generic ranitidine chemically and bio-equivalent.
Adechsa’s ranitidine under Glaxo Group’s good manufacturing practices adds value and comfort.
Zantac priced higher than generics partly due to this added comfort.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. found chemical equivalence but value added by manufacturing practices justifies Zantac’s higher price, per court.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement features and purchase requirement add value to ranitidine beyond generic equivalents.
These features justify recognition in determining arm’s length price for rights and benefits with ranitidine.
Arm’s length comparisons under OECD or other methods require identifying Licence Agreement circumstances linked to Supply Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Licence Agreement features add value justifying recognition in arm’s length price determination after identifying linked circumstances.

propositions.text: Section 69(2) uses 'reasonable amount' reflecting transfer pricing is not exact science, allowing some leeway.
If transfer price is within reasonable range, section requirements are satisfied.
Court may select a point within reasonable range using statistical measures based on relevant evidence.
Comparators will rarely be identical; Tax Court judge must exercise informed judgment for arm’s length price.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 69(2) allows reasonable range in transfer pricing and Tax Court judge must use informed judgment.

propositions.text: Roles of Glaxo Canada and Glaxo Group must be considered in transfer pricing assessment.
Glaxo Canada does secondary manufacturing and marketing; Glaxo Group owns intellectual property and provides rights.
Transfer pricing must not misallocate earnings ignoring different functions, resources, and risks.
Whether compensation for intellectual property rights is justified is for Tax Court judge to determine.

paragraphs.summary: The court states transfer pricing must reflect Glaxo Canada and Group roles; IP compensation is for Tax Court to decide.

propositions.text: Arm’s length prices consider independent interests of both parties to transaction.
Determination under s. 69(2) must reflect interests of both Glaxo Group and Glaxo Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court says arm’s length pricing must consider interests of both Glaxo Group and Glaxo Canada under s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Evidence shows arm’s length distributors prefer ranitidine from Glaxo Group supplier over generic sources.
Higher-than-generic transfer prices may be justified and reasonable under s. 69(2).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence supports higher-than-generic transfer prices as reasonable under s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Dismiss appeal and cross-appeal and remit matter to Rip A.C.J. for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court would dismiss appeal and cross-appeal and remit for redetermination by Rip A.C.J.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada cross-appeals to overturn Federal Court of Appeal's remittal to Tax Court for redetermination.
Glaxo Canada asks to set aside reassessment, claiming it demolished Minister's assumptions.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada cross-appeals, arguing it demolished Minister's assumptions and reassessment should be set aside.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal remitted to Tax Court as Glaxo Canada failed to show prices paid were reasonable under s. 69(2).
Judge erred in law by not applying proper test for reasonable amount if parties dealt at arm’s length.
Federal Court of Appeal declined to determine reasonable amount due to record inadequacy, remitted to Tax Court.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal remitted to Tax Court for redetermination, finding Judge erred and record inadequate for decision.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada argues Minister's choice of generic comparators is basis of assessment.
Burden was only to show generic comparators were improper, which would demolish assessment basis.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada argues burden was only to show generic comparators improper, demolishing assessment basis.

propositions.text: Minister says basis of assessment is that prices paid were unreasonable.
Generic comparators were only a means to show unreasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues assessment basis is unreasonableness of prices, with generic comparators as means to show it.

propositions.text: Basis of assessment found in Minister’s Amended Reply assumptions 14p) and 14r.A).
Assumption 14p): Appellant paid Adechsa price greater than reasonable amount if dealing at arm’s length.
Assumption 14r.A): Amounts paid above other companies’ prices were not for ranitidine supply.

paragraphs.summary: Court states basis of assessment is assumptions 14p) and 14r.A) in Minister’s Amended Reply.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada argues only assumption 14r.A) is basis and it demolished that assumption.
Minister argues basis is assumption 14p).
Text supports Minister’s position that 14p) sets statutory basis under s. 69(2).
Taxpayer liability governed by Act; Minister’s reassessment authority arises from invoking Act provisions.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Minister’s assumption 14p) is basis under s. 69(2); taxpayer liability governed by Act provisions.

propositions.text: In Hickman Motors, taxpayer must demolish exact Minister assumptions but no more.
Assumption 14r.A) was demolished but assumption 14p) was not.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Hickman Motors that taxpayer must demolish exact assumptions; 14r.A) demolished but not 14p).

propositions.text: At Tax Court, Glaxo Canada tried to prove prices reasonable but was unsuccessful.
Glaxo Canada accepted burden to show prices reasonable under s. 69(2).
Success would have demolished assumptions 14p) and 14r.A).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Glaxo Canada tried and failed to prove prices reasonable, which would have demolished assumptions 14p) and 14r.A).

propositions.text: Assumption 14p) that prices paid were greater than reasonable amount remains undemolished.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds assumption 14p) remains standing as prices paid were not shown reasonable.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada argued Federal Court of Appeal could determine reasonable amount.
If Federal Court of Appeal could determine reasonable amount, it could remit to Tax Court for that determination.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada argued Federal Court of Appeal could determine reasonable amount; court agrees it could remit to Tax Court.

propositions.text: Remit matter to Tax Court for redetermination considering Licence Agreement effect on prices.
Tax Court judge should consider new evidence parties seek to adduce and may allow.

paragraphs.summary: Court would remit matter to Tax Court for redetermination considering Licence Agreement and new evidence.

propositions.text: Dismiss appeal with costs; dismiss cross-appeal with costs in this Court; remit to Tax Court for redetermination.
Solicitors for parties identified for appeal and cross-appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses appeal and cross-appeal with costs and remits to Tax Court; identifies solicitors for parties.
